title: The LLC Resonant Converter
subject: Power Electronics
blurb: Why half-bridge LLC exists, what the tank actually does, and how to read the gain curve without guessing.
prerequisites: AC circuit analysis in phasor form

slides.title: You cannot shrink the magnetics without cooking the FETs
slides.lead: Every power supply designer is handed the same instruction: make it smaller. Smaller means higher switching frequency, because transformer and inductor volume falls as frequency rises. That part works. The part that does not work is what happens to the switches.

columns.label: Raise frequency
items: Higher power density, lower BOM volume

columns.label: And you pay for it
items: Switching loss scales directly with frequency
Every turn-on dissipates the energy stored in Coss
Overlap of V and I during transition heats the die
EMI gets worse at exactly the frequencies that matter

slides.note: In a hard-switched converter, switching loss is roughly proportional to frequency. Double the frequency, double the loss. That is the wall. Resonant conversion is the attempt to walk through it.

slides.title: Turn the switch on when its voltage is already zero
slides.lead: Switching loss comes from voltage and current being large at the same instant. If the drain-source voltage has already fallen to zero before the gate rises, the overlap disappears and so does the loss. This is zero voltage switching, and it is the entire reason the LLC topology is shaped the way it is.
slides.caption: Hard switching, top: the gate rises while Vds is still at the rail, and the shaded overlap is energy turned into heat on every cycle. Soft switching, bottom: circulating current in the tank discharges Coss first, so Vds reaches zero before the gate moves. No overlap, no loss.
points: The tank current must be inductive so it lags the voltage and can discharge the output capacitance
That discharge has to finish inside the dead time between the two switches
Get this wrong and you do not merely lose efficiency, you lose the FET

slides.title: Half-bridge, three reactive elements, transformer, rectifier
slides.lead: There is no mystery in the schematic. A half-bridge chops the DC input into a square wave, a three-element tank filters it, a transformer scales and isolates it, and a rectifier turns it back into DC. Everything interesting happens in the tank.

legend.role: Half-bridge. Driven at 50% duty with dead time between them, producing a square wave at the switching node. Duty cycle is fixed — regulation comes from frequency, not from duty.
Resonant capacitor. Series element, also blocks DC so the transformer never sees a DC bias.
Resonant inductor. Often just the transformer leakage inductance, which is why LLC designs are so sensitive to transformer construction.
Magnetizing inductance. Deliberately made small enough to participate in resonance — in a conventional converter you want this large and ignore it. Here it is a design variable.
Transformer. Provides isolation and the turns ratio n that sets the nominal operating point.
Rectifier and output capacitor. The rectifier reflects the load back into the tank as an equivalent AC resistance.

slides.note: Three reactive elements, two inductors and one capacitor, is where the name comes from: L, L, C.

slides.title: There are two resonant frequencies, and everything depends on which one you are near
slides.lead: Most explanations of LLC quote a single resonant frequency and then cannot explain why the gain curve has the shape it does. The circuit has two, and the whole operating map lives between them.

formulas.label: Series resonance
formulas.note: Lm is shorted out by the reflected load, so only Lr and Cr resonate. At this frequency the tank is purely resistive and the gain is 1 regardless of load. This is the design anchor.

formulas.label: Magnetizing resonance
formulas.note: When the secondary stops conducting, Lm is no longer clamped and joins the resonance. Because Lm is much larger than Lr, this frequency is well below fr.

points: fm is always lower than fr, and the ratio between them is set by m = Lm / Lr
Above fr the converter behaves like a series resonant circuit and gain is always below 1
Between fm and fr the converter can boost above 1 — this is the useful region
Below fm the tank turns capacitive, ZVS is lost, and the design fails
slides.note: Hold on to this slide. Every gain curve, operating region and design rule in the rest of this volt is a consequence of these two frequencies and the gap between them.
